text: Over the decades software has become more formalized. Back in the day, writing assembly, everyone was a software engineer. You had to squeeze performance out of everything, using RAM as efficiently as possible. Now everything is broken up, which is both good and bad. I believe it's good because the more experienced spend time on architecture, more junior people implement it. That said, talented junior people are forced to not explore possibilities as much as in the past, which made GREAT software engineers.

text: I was so fortunate.  I worked the whole last half of my career setting my own direction.  I owned a couple systems.  The work I did on those systems, how I did it, when I did it, the design of the work, and the acceptance criteria were all mine to set.  I worked with a couple other teams that used those systems for their own work to determine what was needed, how the APIs into my system should be set up, etc.  I've been retired from that place for almost 5 years now and those are two of the very few systems that haven't given trouble during that whole time.  One of them the last I heard is exactly as I left it.  No work at all has been needed even though the workload has tripled.  I built it to have an order of magnitude of wiggle room so they should be good for a bit yet.  My only advice is if you're working at a place that's trying to funnel you into the "just a coder" role is to leave.  There are plenty of companies that will let you grow and value your skills.  And those places are seldom large corporations.

This is pretty interesting. I've always wondered where I would fall if I were to be categorized in the world of software development. I engineer, develop and code all the software I make, usually with the sole purpose of either solving a problem or automating something. I'm pretty lucky in the fact that I don't usually have to think too hard to see what the problem is and come up with a solution to that problem. I typically find the development part usually requires the most foresight. Not because I'm trying to solve every possible issue that may arise, but I typically try to keep things organized and extensible so that either I or someone else can make changes or add/remove functionality without breaking anything else. The coding is usually the easier part. I can code in about 8 different languages. I don't consider myself to be an expert in any language but I can read nearly any language and understand what's going on. I make frequent commits to create an easy to read audit trail. I test all of my own code, often switching between TDD and BDD (and sometimes "vibe" coding) in the same project.

The most interesting part is, although I've been creating apps/solutions/automation for nearly 30 years and I write code almost every day, I am not nor have I ever been a software developer. I'm not even in that industry. I'm a photographer. I've spent decades developing software to solve my own problems using the best possible practices even though no one else will ever read, modify or touch any of my code. It used to feel like an exercise in futility to me but I've been doing it so long now that it's just natural to me at this point.

text:
In my experience there are two things that really separate 'coders' from 'developers/engineers' that broadly align with the points in the video.

First is whether the prototype/proof-of-concept code they write ready for production. That's not to say that every edge case must be implemented, but the code should properly fit into the relevant software system or pipeline. Put another way, have they thought about how their new code will work in a real environment.

Second, do they actively revise and maintain the codebase. The adage 'If it ain't broke don't fix it' is occasionally true, but in software most often leads to technical debt. A developer/engineer will spend time revising, refactoring, documenting and testing the codebase, just as part of their daily workflow.

text:
I used to give a test I had created for programmming applicants. The test presented a problem and a made up programming language. The test then asked what were the possible solutions, list the tradeoffs and assumptions to the solutions, pick a solution from those and implement it in the provided language. 

The applicants that skipped everything and went straight to a solution (regardless of how good the coded solutions was) - not hired, and that was the vast majority of applicants. 

We had some who attempted basically the "engineering" portion but were unable to do it. 

For those who did the solution evaluation and selection with logical choices and solutions, no matter which solution they chose to actually code, we would hire all other things being equal. We did read the code to make sure it was reasonable but the key was the problem understadning and understanding tradeoffs. 

In the years I administed the test, only one applicant had no experience in the real programming languages we were using but in the design phase stated that "Due to defects in the provided programming language, we can only code this class of solutions." One of the best hires I ever made.

text:
I call myself a software developer because 99% of the time I'm working on a system that has no sure target.  I cannot design or engineer myself to the solution because no one knows what it looks like.  The only way to find the target is to iteratively build it and see what people think.  Refactoring, YAGNI, and a boyscout rule to code quality is critical here.

I view software engineering as something a bit 'harder' in the science sense.  You have a hard target with hard requirements and you should be using methods to hit those targets. You can spend a bit more time on design here because you're more sure of what you're building.

Both types of programming have processes.  You can't do the first without an iterative process.  And I believe the best way to do the 2nd is with an iterative process because that's the best way to confirm what you've built matches what was envisioned.

text:
You don't waste your work when your pull request is denied. That is just the world saying "we don't need your work." And presumably you did the work because YOU need the work, not because you thought SOMEONE ELSE needs the work, so the payoff for you was always going to be that you get what you need. The rest of the world can have what you did for free, if they want it, but if they don't... you don't give a shit. You did it for you. You shared because it costs you nothing to share, and you HAD to do it, but now the next guy doesn't. 

If you really want your pull request added, you can abstract your work out into a plugin or addon for the package, or even fork the project. Nobody can STOP you from releasing your work. And as long as you don't fucking touch the GPL ever for any reason, nobody can MAKE you release it either. 

Most projects migrate from "just let anyone contribute" toward "there is ONE GUY who can commit changes" naturally. It's a sort of intersecting triangles thing: the number of people you LET contribute, which starts at "everybody" and ends at "one guy"... and the number of people who WANT to contribute, which starts at "one guy" and ends at "everybody." When the intersection of these is growing, everyone is happy, but when it starts contracting people get increasingly unhappy. 

Looking back at my experience on the Vista team, this isn't limited to open source. There was a time everyone at Microsoft wanted to put something into Vista, and eventually we had to reduce the team to focus on getting the project out the door.

- First OS to Use Git Version Control System: Linux was developed using the Git version control system, which was initially created by Linus Torvalds to manage the Linux kernel source code. Git has now become the de facto standard for version control.
- First OS to Embrace Containers: Linux introduced Linux Containers (LXC) and later Docker.

I work for a company as the main dev.
We use open source code/libraries.
We contribute bug reports and provide our internal fixes whenever possible, it's not uncommon for later updates to include improved fixes.
Whatever small package that does not include trade secrets or value added piece of code, we publish opensource.
We use licenses (MIT or custom) to segregate code that we let anyone reuse commercially and that we restrict to personal use.
Our time invested publishing and communicating with the authors or maintainers of OSS has given us results manifold. Most common example is to have one staff spend ca 2 hours building a replication scenario for an issue, writing a clear and comprehensive bug report, and setting up a hot fix branch/PR, which results in 3-4 maintainers/users looking into the issue for hours, figuring a proper fix, testing the fix and releasing an update, at no additional cost for us.

Hi there, one of them fans here! (You put my thumbnail in your vid at 5:09, thanks for that by the way! :D) 
Awesome disection of the new season. It's sad to see that your main takeaway is that the new season is 'missing something' but after watching your review I fully agree with your viewpoint. To me, the big issue is that - once again - this was a thirteen episode season, which means you lose on so much of the possible development as a 26-episode season. No surprise then that you put the four seasons that do allow for 26 episodes at the top. For me it's not a big bother JUST YET, purely because of the knowledge of a second season with all the returning cast members, allowing for basically a 26-episode run but spread over two thirteen-episode sagas. The season showed a lot of potential and leaves a to long for and desire from a second season, after which I think we can deffinitevely say if Total Drama is indeed back to its former glory or not.
